title: Vintages and Aging in Burgundy
description: How to read and evaluate Burgundy vintages, the great years for red and white, and understanding how Burgundy evolves in the cellar.
lessons.0.title: How to Read Burgundy Vintages
lessons.0.slides.0.title: How to Read Burgundy Vintages
lessons.0.slides.0.subtitle: 12 minutes
lessons.0.slides.0.description: Why vintages matter more in Burgundy than almost anywhere else — and what shapes the character of each year.
lessons.0.slides.1.title: Why Burgundy Vintages Matter So Much
lessons.0.slides.1.content: Burgundy's marginal cool continental climate makes it uniquely vintage-sensitive. A few centimetres of rain in September, a week of heat in August, or frost in April can completely transform the quality and character of an entire vintage.
lessons.0.slides.1.keyPoints.0: Cool climate: Burgundy is at the northern limit of viable Pinot Noir and Chardonnay cultivation
lessons.0.slides.1.keyPoints.1: Marginal conditions: even a good vintage can include widely varying quality across different villages
lessons.0.slides.1.keyPoints.2: Vertical tasting: comparing different vintages of the same wine is one of the most educational exercises in fine wine
lessons.0.slides.1.keyPoints.3: Climate change impact: since 2000, there have been far more 'great' vintages than in previous decades
lessons.0.slides.2.title: Key Weather Events That Shape Vintages
lessons.0.slides.2.content: Each vintage is shaped by a specific combination of seasonal weather events — each leaves a distinct mark on the wine.
lessons.0.slides.2.keyPoints.0: Spring frost: catastrophic for yield (2021, 2017 frost events destroyed up to 50% of crop)
lessons.0.slides.2.keyPoints.1: Summer heat waves: rapid sugar accumulation, risk of losing acidity (2003, 2020)
lessons.0.slides.2.keyPoints.2: September rain: worst enemy — causes rot, dilution; can ruin a promising vintage
lessons.0.slides.2.keyPoints.3: Cool, even ripening: the ideal — the Goldilocks vintage (2010, 2015, 2019)
lessons.0.slides.3.title: The Concept of 'Vintage Variation' in Burgundy
lessons.0.slides.3.content: Unlike many other wine regions, Burgundy's vintage variation is not simply 'great vs. bad' — it is a stylistic spectrum that reflects the year's particular growing conditions.
lessons.0.slides.3.keyPoints.0: Hot vintages (2003, 2015, 2018): richer, rounder, lower acidity; approachable earlier
lessons.0.slides.3.keyPoints.1: Cool vintages (1996, 2014, 2021): higher acidity, more mineral and structured; require longer aging
lessons.0.slides.3.keyPoints.2: Balanced great vintages (2010, 2019): power AND freshness — the most sought-after profile
lessons.0.slides.3.keyPoints.3: Regional variation: a vintage can be excellent for Chablis but average for Beaune, or vice versa
lessons.0.slides.4.title: 💡 Key Take-aways
lessons.0.slides.4.points.0: 🍷 Burgundy's vintage variation is greater than most wine regions due to its marginal cool climate
lessons.0.slides.4.points.1: 🍷 Not all vintages are 'good or bad' — each reflects a specific stylistic profile shaped by the year's weather
lessons.0.slides.4.points.2: 🍷 Climate change has produced more consistently excellent vintages since 2000
lessons.0.slides.4.points.3: 🍷 Regional variation: Chablis, Côte de Nuits and Côte de Beaune whites may peak in different years
lessons.0.slides.5.title: 🧠 Knowledge Check
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.0.question: Why is vintage variation especially pronounced in Burgundy?
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.0.options.0: A. Because Burgundy vineyards are too large to be affected consistently
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.0.options.1: B. Because Burgundy's cool, marginal climate means small seasonal changes have a large impact on quality and style
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.0.options.2: C. Because Burgundy only uses one grape variety
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.0.options.3: D. Because Burgundy does not allow irrigation
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.0.explanati: Burgundy sits at the northern edge of viable Pinot Noir and Chardonnay cultivation — grapes ripen here only just enough in most years. Because conditions are already marginal, small deviations in temperature, rainfall or sunshine have proportionally enormous effects. A few warm or cool days at critical moments can define the entire vintage.
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.1.question: Which weather event is considered the most damaging for a Burgundy vintage?
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.1.options.1: B. Heavy rainfall in September just before harvest — causing rot and dilution
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.1.options.3: D. Low temperatures during winter dormancy
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.1.explanati: September rain is the most feared weather event in Burgundy. Rain just before harvest causes botrytis (grey rot) to spread rapidly, can dilute previously concentrated juice, and forces difficult decisions about whether to pick early (before rain damage) or wait (risking further rain). The 2012, 2007 and 1992 vintages were all affected by September rain.
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.2.question: How has climate change affected Burgundy vintages since 2000?
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.2.options.0: A. There have been fewer good vintages due to extreme weather
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.2.options.1: B. Rising temperatures have produced more consistently high-quality vintages, though acidity management has become a challenge
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.2.options.2: C. Climate change has had no measurable effect on Burgundy yet
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.2.options.3: D. Cooler vintages are now more frequent
lessons.0.slides.5.questions.2.explanati: Since 2000, Burgundy has had an unprecedented run of fine vintages: 2002, 2005, 2009, 2010, 2012, 2015, 2017, 2018, 2019, 2020, 2022 all scored highly. Rising temperatures help grapes ripen more reliably, reducing the risk of underripe vintages. However, challenges of overripeness, high alcohol and acidity loss have increased.
lessons.1.title: Great Red Burgundy Vintages
lessons.1.slides.0.title: Great Red Burgundy Vintages
lessons.1.slides.0.subtitle: 18 minutes
lessons.1.slides.0.description: The benchmark vintages for Côte d'Or Pinot Noir — what made them special and how they drink today.
lessons.1.slides.1.title: 2015 — The Iconic Modern Vintage
lessons.1.slides.1.content: 2015 is widely considered the greatest Burgundy vintage of the modern era — combining exceptional ripeness with retained freshness and structure.
lessons.1.slides.1.keyPoints.0: Weather: ideal summer with sufficient warmth; no heat extremes; clean September
lessons.1.slides.1.keyPoints.1: Style: rich, opulent, deeply coloured; powerful but balanced; exceptional aromatic complexity
lessons.1.slides.1.keyPoints.2: Drinking window: already approachable; best Grand Cru wines need 10–20 more years
lessons.1.slides.1.keyPoints.3: Critics: described as the 'perfect storm' — the last time Burgundy had this balance was 1990
lessons.1.slides.2.title: 2010 — The Collector's Vintage
lessons.1.slides.2.content: 2010 is the great 'classic' red Burgundy vintage of the 21st century — combining the concentration of a warm year with exceptional freshness and acid balance.
lessons.1.slides.2.keyPoints.0: Weather: hot summer followed by a cool, perfect September — ideal conditions
lessons.1.slides.2.keyPoints.1: Style: more structured and linear than 2015; darker, deeper; exceptional tannic framework
lessons.1.slides.2.keyPoints.2: Drinking window: most Grands Crus still need 10–15 more years (until 2030–35)
lessons.1.slides.2.keyPoints.3: Comparison: 2010 = the intellectual vintage; 2015 = the sensuous vintage
lessons.1.slides.3.title: 2005 and 1999 — The Modern Classics
lessons.1.slides.3.content: Two different but outstanding vintages representing the early 21st century and the final decade of the 20th.
lessons.1.slides.3.keyPoints.0: 2005: powerful, structured, concentrated; now drinking beautifully at Grand Cru level (drink 2020–35)
lessons.1.slides.3.keyPoints.1: 1999: a slightly underrated vintage; generous, pure Pinot fruit; less structured than 2005 but very beautiful
lessons.1.slides.3.keyPoints.2: 1999: now in its drinking window for most wines; exceptional DRC, Rousseau from this year
lessons.1.slides.3.keyPoints.3: 2005 is often cited as the first vintage of the 'modern era' of great Burgundy
lessons.1.slides.4.title: 1996 and 1990 — The Classic Era
lessons.1.slides.4.content: Two of the greatest Burgundy vintages of the 20th century — each defining the style of its era.
lessons.1.slides.4.keyPoints.0: 1996: high acidity, structured, mineral — the perfect 'old school' Burgundy vintage
lessons.1.slides.4.keyPoints.1: 1996: now in its drinking window; top Grands Crus still magnificent but need to be consumed in the next 15 years
lessons.1.slides.4.keyPoints.2: 1990: arguably the greatest Burgundy vintage of the second half of the 20th century — rich, concentrated, explosive
lessons.1.slides.4.keyPoints.3: 1990 Grands Crus: now at peak (drink 2020–2035); beyond 2035 only for the greatest wines
lessons.1.slides.5.title: 💡 Key Take-aways
lessons.1.slides.5.points.0: 🍷 2015 = the greatest modern red Burgundy vintage; 2010 = the great structured classic
lessons.1.slides.5.points.1: 🍷 1990 and 1996 remain two of the greatest 20th-century red Burgundy vintages
lessons.1.slides.5.points.2: 🍷 Great Burgundy vintages require patient cellaring — 10–20 years for Grand Cru
lessons.1.slides.5.points.3: 🍷 Understanding a vintage's style (opulent vs. structured) helps predict when it will peak
lessons.1.slides.6.title: 🧠 Knowledge Check
lessons.1.slides.6.questions.0.question: What characterises the 2010 red Burgundy vintage?
lessons.1.slides.6.questions.0.options.0: A. Rich and opulent; already approachable and drinking beautifully now
lessons.1.slides.6.questions.0.options.1: B. Structured, linear, deep; exceptional tannic framework; still needs time in 2024
lessons.1.slides.6.questions.0.options.2: C. Light and delicate; early-drinking; best drunk young
lessons.1.slides.6.questions.0.options.3: D. Problematic high alcohol; lacks balance
lessons.1.slides.6.questions.0.explanati: 2010 is the archetypal 'classic' red Burgundy vintage — combining concentration from the warm summer with remarkable freshness from the cool September. The resulting wines are structured, precise and linear, built for long aging. Most Grand Cru wines will not reach their peak until the 2030s.
lessons.1.slides.6.questions.1.question: Which vintage is most often cited as the greatest of the modern era for red Burgundy?
lessons.1.slides.6.questions.1.explanati: 2015 is widely regarded as the greatest modern red Burgundy vintage — a 'perfect storm' of exceptional ripeness, freshness and aromatic complexity. Many critics compare it to the legendary 1990. Grand Cru wines from this vintage are expected to drink well into the 2040s and 2050s.
lessons.1.slides.6.questions.2.question: How does 2015 compare stylistically to 2010 for red Burgundy?
lessons.1.slides.6.questions.2.options.0: A. 2015 is more structured and austere; 2010 is more opulent
lessons.1.slides.6.questions.2.options.1: B. 2015 is more opulent and sensuous; 2010 is more structured, intellectual and precise
lessons.1.slides.6.questions.2.options.2: C. The two vintages are virtually identical in style
lessons.1.slides.6.questions.2.options.3: D. 2010 is the drinking-now vintage; 2015 needs 40 years
lessons.1.slides.6.questions.2.explanati: The 2015 vs. 2010 debate is one of the most discussed in Burgundy. 2015 is the 'sensuous' vintage — rich, opulent, immediately seductive. 2010 is the 'intellectual' vintage — structured, precise, less immediately generous but potentially more age-worthy. Collectors often buy both to observe how they evolve differently.
lessons.1.slides.6.questions.3.question: What makes 1990 stand out as a Burgundy vintage?
lessons.1.slides.6.questions.3.options.0: A. It produced the highest quantity of wine in the 20th century
lessons.1.slides.6.questions.3.options.1: B. It is widely regarded as the greatest red Burgundy vintage of the second half of the 20th century — rich, concentrated and explosive
lessons.1.slides.6.questions.3.options.2: C. It is a structurally similar vintage to 2010
lessons.1.slides.6.questions.3.options.3: D. It was the first vintage where Pinot Noir fully ripened in Burgundy
lessons.1.slides.6.questions.3.explanati: 1990 is often called the greatest red Burgundy of the second half of the 20th century. An extraordinarily hot and dry summer produced concentrated, opulent wines with exceptional depth and longevity. The finest Grands Crus — DRC, Rousseau, Leroy — from this vintage are now in their prime (2020–2035) and command extraordinary prices at auction.
lessons.1.slides.7.title: Summary
lessons.1.slides.7.content: Burgundy's great red vintages reveal the region's extraordinary capacity: from the structured precision of 1996 and 2010 to the voluptuous grandeur of 1990 and 2015. The collector who understands these vintages holds the key to unlocking red Burgundy's full potential.
lessons.2.title: Great White Burgundy Vintages
lessons.2.slides.0.title: Great White Burgundy Vintages
lessons.2.slides.0.subtitle: 12 minutes
lessons.2.slides.0.description: The benchmark vintages for Burgundy Chardonnay — and why white and red are not always great in the same year.
lessons.2.slides.1.title: White vs Red: Different Vintage Needs
lessons.2.slides.1.content: White and red Burgundy are not always exceptional in the same vintage. A year that produces great red wine (long warm summer for Pinot Noir ripeness) may be less suitable for Chardonnay, which needs more freshness and acidity.
lessons.2.slides.1.keyPoints.0: Chardonnay ripens earlier than Pinot Noir — whites are typically harvested 1–2 weeks earlier
lessons.2.slides.1.keyPoints.1: Warm vintages: great for reds; whites may lack acidity and age prematurely
lessons.2.slides.1.keyPoints.2: Cool, balanced vintages: often excellent for whites (1996, 2014, 2022) even if reds are less impressive
lessons.2.slides.1.keyPoints.3: Chablis vs Côte de Beaune: can vary greatly in the same vintage due to different terroir and microclimate
lessons.2.slides.2.title: Great White Burgundy Vintages
lessons.2.slides.2.content: A selection of the benchmark vintages for white Burgundy, each with its distinct character.
lessons.2.slides.2.keyPoints.0: 2014: possibly the greatest modern vintage for white Burgundy — razor-sharp acidity, extraordinary mineral tension, exceptional longevity
lessons.2.slides.2.keyPoints.1: 2017: rich and generous; more immediately accessible; excellent from Meursault and Puligny
lessons.2.slides.2.keyPoints.2: 2019: the 'complete' vintage — power and freshness combined; outstanding for both red and white
lessons.2.slides.2.keyPoints.3: 2012: powerful whites; mineral and structured; still drinking beautifully now
lessons.2.slides.3.title: White Burgundy Aging: The Premox Problem
lessons.2.slides.3.content: A significant challenge emerged in the 1990s–2000s: premature oxidation (premox) — white Burgundies turning brown and oxidised far before their expected life.
lessons.2.slides.3.keyPoints.0: Premox: white Burgundy developing amber colour and sherry-like oxidative notes within 5–10 years of bottling
lessons.2.slides.3.keyPoints.1: Cause: combination of reduced sulphur use, lighter corks, and possible leaky stoppers in the 1990s–2005 period
lessons.2.slides.3.keyPoints.2: Most affected vintages: 1996–2006 whites (though some excellent bottles exist)
lessons.2.slides.3.keyPoints.3: Solution: most producers now use better corks and slightly increased SO₂; premox is less common since 2010
lessons.2.slides.4.title: 💡 Key Take-aways
lessons.2.slides.4.points.0: 🍷 White Burgundy has different vintage needs from red — acidity preservation is paramount
lessons.2.slides.4.points.1: 🍷 2014 is widely regarded as the greatest modern white Burgundy vintage
lessons.2.slides.4.points.2: 🍷 Premature oxidation (premox) affected 1996–2006 white Burgundies — check bottles carefully before serving
lessons.2.slides.4.points.3: 🍷 The same vintage can be outstanding for Chablis and only average for Meursault — regional variation matters
lessons.2.slides.5.title: 🧠 Knowledge Check
lessons.2.slides.5.questions.0.question: Why is 2014 often considered the greatest modern vintage for white Burgundy?
lessons.2.slides.5.questions.0.options.0: A. It produced the highest quantity of white wine ever recorded
lessons.2.slides.5.questions.0.options.1: B. A perfect growing season produced whites of extraordinary acidity, mineral tension and longevity
lessons.2.slides.5.questions.0.options.2: C. 2014 was extremely hot, producing very ripe whites
lessons.2.slides.5.questions.0.options.3: D. 2014 was the first year without premox problems
lessons.2.slides.5.questions.0.explanati: 2014 is celebrated for producing white Burgundies of exceptional freshness and precision. A difficult flowering period reduced yields (increasing concentration) while a cool, extended growing season preserved natural acidity and developed extraordinary aromatic complexity. These wines are built for very long aging — top Grand Cru should drink well into the 2040s.
lessons.2.slides.5.questions.1.question: What is 'premox' in white Burgundy?
lessons.2.slides.5.questions.1.options.0: A. A type of malolactic fermentation specific to white wine
lessons.2.slides.5.questions.1.options.1: B. Premature oxidation — white Burgundy turning amber and sherry-like within 5–10 years of bottling
lessons.2.slides.5.questions.1.options.2: C. A deliberate winemaking technique to add oxidative character
lessons.2.slides.5.questions.1.options.3: D. A type of reduction fault
lessons.2.slides.5.questions.1.explanati: Premature oxidation (premox) refers to white Burgundy wines developing amber colour, oxidised aromas (sherry-like, nutty, stale) and loss of freshness within 5–10 years of release — far earlier than expected. It became a significant quality issue in the 1990s and 2000s and affected wines from virtually all top producers. The likely cause was insufficient cork quality combined with reduced sulphur use.
lessons.2.slides.5.questions.2.question: In a warm Burgundy vintage, which type of wine generally benefits more?
lessons.2.slides.5.questions.2.options.0: A. Chardonnay whites, which thrive in heat
lessons.2.slides.5.questions.2.options.1: B. Red wines (Pinot Noir), which achieve better ripeness and depth
lessons.2.slides.5.questions.2.options.2: C. There is no difference between reds and whites in warm vintages
lessons.2.slides.5.questions.2.options.3: D. Chablis benefits most from heat
lessons.2.slides.5.questions.2.explanati: In warm vintages, Pinot Noir benefits — achieving the phenolic ripeness and depth it often struggles to reach in Burgundy's cool climate. Chardonnay, however, may lose acidity too rapidly and produce whites that are initially rich but lack the freshness and mineral tension needed for long aging. Cool and balanced vintages often favour whites more.
lessons.3.title: How Burgundy Ages and When to Drink
lessons.3.slides.0.title: How Burgundy Ages and When to Drink
lessons.3.slides.0.subtitle: 15 minutes
lessons.3.slides.0.description: Understanding Burgundy's aging trajectory — how it evolves, when it peaks, and how to know when a wine is ready.
lessons.3.slides.1.title: The Aging Curve: Burgundy Red
lessons.3.slides.1.content: Fine red Burgundy follows a distinctive aging arc — from youthful primary fruit through a 'dumb' closed phase to a magnificent secondary and tertiary complexity.
lessons.3.slides.1.keyPoints.0: 0–5 years: youthful red fruits, primary florals; charming but not complex
lessons.3.slides.1.keyPoints.1: 5–10 years: tannins close up; wine becomes 'dumb' — less expressive; patience required
lessons.3.slides.1.keyPoints.2: 10–15 years: secondary complexity begins — forest floor, earth, mushroom, dried fruits emerge
lessons.3.slides.1.keyPoints.3: 15–25+ years (Grand Cru): peak complexity — silk, undergrowth, truffle, dried rose; ethereal persistence
lessons.3.slides.2.title: The Aging Curve: Burgundy White
lessons.3.slides.2.content: Great white Burgundy ages very differently from red — its arc is shorter and it peaks earlier, yet the finest whites can last 20–30 years.
lessons.3.slides.2.keyPoints.0: 0–3 years: youthful Chardonnay — citrus, white flowers, vanilla and toasty oak dominant
lessons.3.slides.2.keyPoints.1: 3–8 years: primary character fades; honeyed, hazelnut and mineral complexity emerges
lessons.3.slides.2.keyPoints.2: 8–15 years (Premier/Grand Cru): peak complexity — beeswax, dried honey, truffle, white mushroom
lessons.3.slides.2.keyPoints.3: 15–25+ years (Grand Cru only): extraordinary aged character — Meursault, Montrachet can reach transcendence
lessons.3.slides.3.title: Reading Cellar Potential by Classification Level
lessons.3.slides.3.content: Not all Burgundy needs or benefits from aging. Understanding what to cellar vs drink young is critical.
lessons.3.slides.3.keyPoints.0: Regional Bourgogne: drink within 3–5 years (red), 2–4 years (white)
lessons.3.slides.3.keyPoints.3: Grand Cru: 12–25 years (red), 10–20 years (white) — exceptional wines 30+ years
lessons.3.slides.4.title: Serving Burgundy at Its Best
lessons.3.slides.4.content: Proper service maximises the enjoyment of aged Burgundy — temperature, decanting and glassware all play a role.
lessons.3.slides.4.keyPoints.0: Red Burgundy serving temperature: 15–17°C (too warm = alcohol-heavy; too cold = aromas muted)
lessons.3.slides.4.keyPoints.1: White Burgundy temperature: 12–14°C (not too cold — cold suppresses complexity)
lessons.3.slides.4.keyPoints.2: Decanting young Burgundy: gentle decanting helps open up closed young wines (30 min for youthful reds)
lessons.3.slides.4.keyPoints.3: Aged Burgundy: minimal decanting — fragile complexity can dissipate quickly; stand upright 24h before serving
lessons.3.slides.5.title: 💡 Key Take-aways
lessons.3.slides.5.points.0: 🍷 Red Burgundy goes through a 'dumb' closed phase (5–10 years) before secondary complexity emerges
lessons.3.slides.5.points.1: 🍷 Grand Cru red Burgundy needs 12–25 years to reach its peak; the greatest wines need 30+ years
lessons.3.slides.5.points.2: 🍷 White Burgundy peaks earlier but can last 20+ years at Grand Cru level
lessons.3.slides.5.points.3: 🍷 Regional and Village Burgundy is designed to be enjoyed within 5–8 years — no need to cellar
lessons.3.slides.6.title: 🧠 Knowledge Check
lessons.3.slides.6.questions.0.question: What is the 'dumb' phase in red Burgundy aging?
lessons.3.slides.6.questions.0.options.0: A. The phase immediately after harvest when the wine is still fermenting
lessons.3.slides.6.questions.0.options.1: B. A period approximately 5–10 years after bottling when the wine closes up and becomes less expressive
lessons.3.slides.6.questions.0.options.2: C. A permanent state of oxidation
lessons.3.slides.6.questions.0.options.3: D. The period when Burgundy is best served at low temperature
lessons.3.slides.6.questions.0.explanati: The 'dumb' phase is a well-known phenomenon in fine red wine aging, particularly red Burgundy. After an initially charming youthful phase (0–5 years), tannins and other structural compounds begin to bind, causing the wine to close up and seem less expressive. Patience is required — 5–10 more years are usually needed before secondary complexity (earthy, forest floor, truffle) begins to emerge.
lessons.3.slides.6.questions.1.question: How long should a great Grand Cru red Burgundy be cellared before reaching its peak?
lessons.3.slides.6.questions.1.options.2: C. 12–25 years (sometimes 30+ years for the greatest wines)
lessons.3.slides.6.questions.1.options.3: D. No cellaring needed — drink immediately
lessons.3.slides.6.questions.1.explanati: Grand Cru red Burgundy (Chambertin, Musigny, Romanée-Conti) is built for long aging. Most Grands Crus from great vintages need 12–25 years to reach peak complexity, with the finest wines (Romanée-Conti, La Tâche, Chambertin from 1990, 2010, 2015) capable of developing for 30–40 years.
lessons.3.slides.6.questions.2.question: At what temperature should red Burgundy ideally be served?
lessons.3.slides.6.questions.2.explanati: Red Burgundy is ideally served at 15–17°C — slightly below most people's 'room temperature'. At 20°C or above, alcohol becomes too prominent and the delicate Pinot Noir fruit is overwhelmed by heat. At below 13°C, the aromatics are suppressed and tannins seem harsh. The 'slightly cool cellar temperature' ideal applies perfectly to Burgundy's delicate Pinot Noir.
lessons.3.slides.6.questions.3.question: Why should aged Burgundy be decanted with caution?
lessons.3.slides.6.questions.3.options.0: A. Aged Burgundy has too much tannin to decant
lessons.3.slides.6.questions.3.options.1: B. The fragile complexity of aged Burgundy can dissipate quickly when exposed to too much oxygen
lessons.3.slides.6.questions.3.options.2: C. Decanting removes the sediment permanently
lessons.3.slides.6.questions.3.options.3: D. Aged Burgundy should always be decanted for 6 hours
lessons.3.slides.6.questions.3.explanati: Aged Burgundy is one of the most delicate wines to handle. Its complex tertiary aromas — dried roses, forest floor, truffles, mushroom — can begin to dissipate within an hour of exposure to oxygen. Extended decanting can literally cause the wine to 'fade' before your eyes. For aged Grand Cru Burgundy, standing the bottle upright for 24 hours and decanting briefly (just to separate sediment) is usually the best approach.
lessons.3.slides.7.title: Summary
lessons.3.slides.7.content: Understanding when and how Burgundy ages is the foundation of a serious collection. Patient cellaring, careful vintage selection and attentive service transform an already fine wine into one of the most transcendent experiences in all of gastronomy. The greatest Burgundies reward the wait — but they demand it first.
